item.title: How Much Money Do You Need to Be Financially Free?
item.description:
The internet never lacks an answer to this question. Someone says five million is enough; someone else says a hundred million. These numbers contradict each other less because somebody did the arithmetic wrong than because the word “freedom” was never defined.

In this video, 小Lin说 offers a version that can actually be calculated, and it comes down to a single multiplier: take your monthly spending and multiply it by 480. I re-derived the equation and filled in the parts the video left out.

What “freedom” means

“Not working, living off savings for the rest of your life” hides three conditions that must hold at the same time:

  1. No work. You no longer sell your time for money.
  2. No loss of purchasing power. Today’s standard of living persists until death, not bare survival.
  3. No end date. Not “enough to last until 85”.

The third is the one that quietly gets swapped out. Most “save X and retire” calculations are actually finite-horizon: spend until a certain age, end at zero. That is perfectly reasonable, but the answer becomes much smaller, as we will see.

All three conditions together describe something standard in finance: a perpetuity. You spend only the real return each year and never touch the principal. Money like that does not run out.

How much principal sits behind CNY 10,000 a month

Perpetuity: the principal stays intact

Let \(X\) be monthly spending at today’s prices. Because prices rise, \(X\) rises with them; in real terms it is a flat line costing \(12X\) a year.

Let \(F\) be assets and \(r\) the annual return after inflation. For the real value of assets not to fall, one year of real return must exactly cover one year of spending:

$$ rF = 12X \quad\Longrightarrow\quad F = \frac{12X}{r} = 12X \cdot \frac{1}{r}. $$

With \(r = 2.5\%\):

$$ F = \frac{12X}{0.025} = 480X. $$

The mysterious 480 has no other secret: it is \(12 \div 0.025\).

The 480 is not an amount but a multiplier. Its job is to translate “how much per month” into “how much in total”:

Monthly spending \(X\) Threshold assets \(480X\)
CNY 3,000 CNY 1.44M
CNY 5,000 CNY 2.40M
CNY 10,000 CNY 4.80M
CNY 20,000 CNY 9.60M
CNY 30,000 CNY 14.40M

There is a more useful reading of the same number: CNY 480 of assets buys CNY 1 of permanent monthly income. Any permanent increase of CNY 100 a month in spending therefore requires another CNY 48,000 of assets. A CNY 100 monthly subscription is worth CNY 48,000 on a perpetual basis.

Finite horizon: the principal may be spent

Release the “no shrinkage” constraint and the question becomes a different one: how long does the money last?

With monthly spending \(X\), real return \(r\) and initial assets \(F\), requiring the balance to reach exactly zero at the end of year \(T\):

$$ F = 12X \cdot \frac{1 - (1+r)^{-T}}{r}. $$

As \(T \to \infty\), \((1+r)^{-T}\) tends to zero and the expression collapses to \(F = 12X / r\), the 480 version. So 480 is an upper bound, not a lower one; the shorter the horizon, the less you need:

Horizon Coverage multiplier Needed at CNY 10,000/month
30 years 251 CNY 2.51M
50 years 340 CNY 3.40M
Perpetual 480 CNY 4.80M

Thirty years and perpetuity differ by nearly half. That is the distance between “enough until 85” and “never runs out”.

Loading calculator…

CNY 6M, CNY 20,000 a month, 2.5% real: annual spending of CNY 240,000 exceeds the CNY 150,000 real return, the gap comes out of principal, and the balance reaches zero in about 39.7 years. On a perpetual basis the same portfolio supports CNY 12,500 a month. That gap of CNY 7,500 is the price of the promise that the principal never moves.

The 4% rule is the back-tested version of the same equation. The familiar rule (Bengen, the Trinity study) says that withdrawing 4% of a portfolio each year has historically survived 30 years. As a multiplier that is 25 times annual spending, or 300 times monthly spending, which places it between the 30-year (251×) and 50-year (340×) rows in the table above. It is not a different calculation; the difference is where the numbers come from. We fix the real return and solve for the principal; the rule tries historical sequences and asks which withdrawal survived the worst thirty years.

Put 4% back into the equation — 30 years, 4% withdrawn, balance at zero — and the implied real return is only about 1.2%. That does not mean the rule assumes 1.2%; the average real return behind it is far higher. It means volatility and unlucky starting years consume the difference, so the effect is to spend a 5% return as though it were 1.2%.

The extra 49× is the price of volatility. Over the same 30 years, a certain 2.5% needs only 251×, while the historical backtest needs 300×. Those 49 multiples buy insurance against not knowing which year you start in, which is sequence risk. Read the other way, 251× is the ideal case: in the real world a 2.5% return with volatility over 30 years drifts toward 300×. The figure is itself being revised down — Morningstar’s 2025 safe withdrawal rate for 30 years is 3.9% (Morningstar) and Bengen’s own 2024 number is 4.7% — so it is safer to read as an upper bound than as a promise.

What the chart actually shows

Loading calculator…

The most useful thing about this chart is not that it produces 480 but that it shows how fragile the number is. The curve rises steeply on the left and flattens on the right; the three lines bunch together on the right and only separate on the left.

  • The lower the return, the more an error costs.

    • The multiple is inversely proportional to the real return, so a one-point disagreement in \(r\) moves the answer relatively by about \(1/r\): a tenth near 8%, half near 2% — and this is also the stretch hardest to judge.
    • \(X\) is on your bank statements, and the money for children and housing has a market price, but \(r\) is guesswork, and it is exactly the term that gets magnified most. The 480 is, in the end, the reading of an assumption.

  • The higher the return, the less the horizon matters.

    • Whatever principal is left after 30 years shrinks quickly in present value as returns rise, so perpetuity and 30 years converge.
    • Perpetuity needs \(1/[1-(1+r)^{-30}]\) times the assets of a 30-year horizon: 1.11× at 8%, 2.23× at 2%, 3.87× at 1%.
    • The same preference for never touching the principal costs almost nothing at high returns and a great deal at low ones; the return is what prices it.

  • Only \(X\) and the horizon are yours to set.

    • Returns come from the market, not from effort, so the sensible order is: record twelve months of spending first, so that \(X\) is a figure from statements; then fix the horizon as a specific year rather than “forever”; and only then decide on \(r\), taking its lower end.
    • The number that falls out is not a target to reach but what suffices under one assumption.

Why it must be the real return

Nominal and real returns are separated by inflation. Write the nominal return as \(n\), inflation as \(i\) and the real return as \(r\); the relationship is not subtraction but Fisher’s equation:

$$ 1 + r = \frac{1 + n}{1 + i} \quad\Longrightarrow\quad r = \frac{1 + n}{1 + i} - 1. $$

With a 4.5% nominal return and 2% inflation, \(r = 1.045 / 1.02 - 1 = 2.45\%\), which gives a multiplier of 489.6 rather than 480. The difference is small, but the concept is not: what must be preserved is purchasing power, not a nominal balance.

Fixed deposits make the arithmetic concrete. Roughly current levels: 0.95% for one year, 1.3% for five years, and core inflation around 1.0%.

$$ \begin{aligned} r_{5y} &= \frac{1.013}{1.01} - 1 = 0.30\%,\\ r_{1y} &= \frac{1.0095}{1.01} - 1 = -0.05\%. \end{aligned} $$

Five-year deposits beat inflation by a hair. One-year deposits already lose in real terms. This is not merely a “low return” problem. When \(r \le 0\), \(1/r\) diverges, and the perpetuity does not exist at all: no amount of money preserves its purchasing power.

So “keep it all in the bank” is ruled out by the equation itself. It does not ask you to trade stocks; it only asks for a positive real return.

Where 2.5% comes from.

Do not use US equity data. The textbook “8% long-run stock return” comes from US markets and does not transfer to Chinese equities. Anyone who has invested in A-shares has that intuition, and the intuition is right.

Look at domestic institutions’ long-run record. China’s enterprise annuities returned about 6.17% a year on average from 2007 to 2024 (the video’s figure). That is the record of professional fund managers.

Subtract fees. Management, custody, subscription, redemption and advisory costs, explicit and implicit, typically take another two to three percentage points before reaching an individual investor. Six percent arriving as under four is the normal case.

Subtract inflation. With long-run inflation at 2%, a 4%–4.5% nominal return corresponds to 2%–2.5% real. Taking the upper bound gives 480.

In fairness: 2.5% is a conservative assumption. Global equity markets have historically delivered real returns near 5%, and that would give a multiplier of 240. Choosing the conservative value means deducting the margin for “things go worse than planned” up front, in exchange for a number that still works if you are pessimistic.

Additive terms: children, health, housing

The 480 covers day-to-day spending only. The equation also has three additive terms:

$$ F = 480X + KN + M + H. $$

They do not belong inside \(X\). Everyday spending runs evenly year by year, whereas these three land in a few particular years; folding them into \(X\) would turn a smooth line into a few spikes and the multiplier would stop meaning anything. Each is treated in turn.

Children, \(KN\). \(K\) is the lifetime cost per child, \(N\) the number. The China Fertility Cost Report cited in the video puts the 2024 national average at about CNY 2,544 per child per month, or roughly CNY 580,000 to age 18, including pregnancy; about CNY 1.0M in Beijing, CNY 1.08M in Shanghai and CNY 430,000 in Guizhou. Regional differences track GDP per capita closely. The report also notes that China’s cost relative to GDP per capita is the second highest in the world, after South Korea.

This is the item most often underestimated, because CNY 580,000 stops at 18. University fees, study abroad and a down payment on a home are not in it. The video’s scope is 18 years; anything beyond has to be added by hand. The scale effect of “each additional child cuts average cost by 15%” is explicitly ignored, and the equation does not reflect it either: apply your own coefficient if you want it.

Health, \(M\). The video estimates CNY 150,000–300,000 over a lifetime in a second-tier city and CNY 300,000–600,000 in a first-tier city. The variance here is enormous and the upper bound is open, so this is a reserve rather than a budget.

Housing, \(H\). Add the market price in your target city directly, with no inflation or investment adjustment. If you already own a home, add nothing; if you plan to rent forever, put the rent into \(X\).

Retirement is not listed separately. \(X\) already includes the right to spend until the end of time. A more careful treatment would lower day-to-day consumption in old age while raising care costs; the video averages the two out with a single \(X\), which is a reasonable simplification.

Worked examples

The national urban average. In 2025, urban household consumption per capita was CNY 35,869 a year, or CNY 2,989 a month (National Bureau of Statistics). That definition already includes housing, health and education, so the later items are not added again:

$$ F = 480 \times 2{,}989 \approx \text{CNY } 1.435\text{M}. $$

One person needs about CNY 1.44M; a couple about CNY 2.87M. On the all-household measure the figure is lower: consumption per capita was CNY 29,476 a year, CNY 2,456 a month, corresponding to CNY 1.18M.

A family of four in a first-tier city. Monthly spending of CNY 15,000, two children at CNY 1.5M each, CNY 1.5M reserved for the couple’s health, and a 120 m² home worth CNY 7M:

Item Amount
Ongoing spending \(480 \times 1.5\) CNY 7.20M
Children \(1.5 \times 2\) CNY 3.00M
Health CNY 1.50M
Housing CNY 7.00M
Total CNY 18.70M

Look at the structure: only 38% is the perpetual part, and 62% is three one-off outlays. For most families, housing and children determine that number far more than the return assumption does.

Solving backwards. With CNY 6M, one child at CNY 700,000 and CNY 500,000 for health, no home purchase:

$$ \begin{aligned} 480X &= 600 - 70 - 50 = 480,\\ X &= \text{CNY } 10{,}000 \text{ a month}. \end{aligned} $$

No children, a CNY 1.2M home, and still CNY 500,000 for health:

$$ \begin{aligned} 480X &= 600 - 120 - 50 = 430,\\ X &\approx \text{CNY } 9{,}000 \text{ a month}. \end{aligned} $$

(The video’s second example gives CNY 9,000, which only reconciles if the CNY 500,000 health reserve is deducted as well; deducting the home price alone gives CNY 10,000. That is the only discrepancy I found when re-checking the arithmetic.)

“Six million and I can only spend nine thousand a month?” The reaction is understandable. The cost comes from that premise: assets must not shrink by a single yuan. Let the asset decline and the same CNY 6M supports far more spending, at the price of writing a depletion year into the plan.

The cases above all use fixed parameters. Swap in your own spending, children and housing, and work it through in the panel below.

item.title: Map First, Then Move
item.description:
A few days ago I listened to an episode with Justin Sun. He described buying property: look at a hundred apartments first, don’t rush to transact. Then a smaller version: ten apartments, buy too early and you may miss a better one, buy too late and the earlier ones are gone — so which one do you take? He also mentioned the golden ratio, 0.618.

The direction is right. The number is not. Those remarks stack several different theories on top of one another: sometimes the secretary problem, sometimes search theory, sometimes the value of information, and underneath it all explore versus exploit. They are usually discussed as one thing, while answering different questions. So let me take them in order.

The secretary problem, starting from ten apartments

The setup

Suppose you run a company and need to hire the strongest of 100 candidates, under these rules:

  • You know the total number of candidates in advance.
  • Candidates are interviewed in a completely random order.
  • After each interview you can rank that candidate against everyone interviewed so far.
  • You must decide hire or reject immediately after each interview.
  • A rejection cannot be reversed.
  • A hire ends the process at once.
  • The only objective is to hire the single best candidate.

The question: which strategy maximises the probability of hiring the best one?

The answer is not the 80/20 rule, not a 50/50 split, and not the golden ratio. It is the reciprocal of Euler’s number:

$$ \frac{1}{e}\approx 36.79\% $$

This is the 37% rule. Its structure has two phases: pure exploration to build a benchmark, then a selection phase in which you act on the first opportunity that beats everything seen so far.

Why exactly 37%

Let there be $n$ candidates, with the first $r$ observed and rejected; afterwards you hire the first person better than everyone before. Let the global best appear at position $k$.

Success requires two things at once: the best arrives after the observation window, $k>r$; and among the first $k-1$ candidates the best one falls inside the first $r$ — otherwise you would have hired someone else earlier.

Since the order is random, the probability the best sits at position $k$ is $1/n$; the probability that the best of the first $k-1$ lies within the first $r$ is $r/(k-1)$. Summing over all successful cases:

$$ P(r)=\sum_{k=r+1}^{n}\frac{1}{n}\cdot\frac{r}{k-1} =\frac{r}{n}\sum_{k=r+1}^{n}\frac{1}{k-1} $$

For large $n$ the sum becomes an integral; with $x=r/n$:

$$ P(x)\approx -x\ln x $$

Differentiating:

$$ P'(x)=-\ln x-1 $$

Setting it to zero gives $x^*=1/e$, and since $P’’(x)=-1/x<0$ this is a maximum. Substituting back:

$$ P(x^*)=\frac{1}{e}\approx 36.79\% $$

The optimal observation fraction and the asymptotic optimal success probability are the same number. What it means concretely: even with a million candidates this strategy still lands the best one with probability near 37%, while picking at random gives one in a million.

Behaviour at finite sample sizes

The 37% above is a large-sample approximation. With finite populations the exact optimum shifts slightly. Using the asymptotic curve for $n=100$, the success rate by observation fraction is:

Fraction observed Probability of picking the best
5% 15.0%
10% 23.0%
20% 32.2%
30% 36.1%
36.79% 36.79%
38.2% (1 − golden ratio) 36.8%
50% 34.7%
61.8% (golden ratio) 29.7%
80% 17.9%
90% 9.5%

With the exact formula instead, the optimum for 10 candidates is to observe and reject 3 (30.0%), succeeding 39.87% of the time — slightly above the asymptotic value. As the population grows the exact fraction converges to $1/e$: at 100 the optimum is 37 observed, with 37.10%; at 1000 it is 368, with 36.82%.

Two things stand out. First, observing 61.8% yields only 29.7% — the golden ratio is clearly worse than simply looking at a third, and worse than 50%. But its complement, 38.2%, is almost exactly optimal at 36.8%. If 0.618 refers to the share left for selection rather than the share observed, the number is very close to correct — probably why 0.618 and 37% keep appearing in the same conversation. Second, the optimum is flat: 30% and 36.79% differ by less than one percentage point. So there is no reason to carry 36.79% around to two decimals; what the number says is “roughly a third”.

Loading interactive demo…

Why observing too much hurts

Split success into two multiplied factors:

  • the probability that the global best has not yet been passed over;
  • the probability of correctly recognising and taking the best, given that it has not been passed over.

The more you observe, the more reliable your benchmark, so the second factor rises. But the chance that the best is already behind you also rises, so the first factor falls. Their product produces an interior optimum.

Behind this sits a more general regularity: accumulating information and preserving opportunities are not aligned objectives. To obtain more information you sometimes have to give up opportunities you already hold.

From the secretary problem to optimal stopping

The secretary problem is elegant but its assumptions are harsh: fixed population, no going back, relative rank only, no need to judge absolute value, no room for good enough. In real life almost none of them hold.

The general form

Suppose at time $t$ you receive new information, forming the information set $\mathcal{F}_{t}$, and decide whether to stop. Let $\tau$ be the stopping time, $R_\tau$ the payoff from acting, $C_\tau$ the accumulated search cost. The objective is

$$ \sup_{\tau\in\mathcal{T}}\ \mathbb{E}\left[R_\tau-C_\tau\right] $$

What is optimised is not a fixed choice but a policy that decides, from the information in hand, when to stop.

As dynamic programming this means comparing two values: the payoff from acting now, $g_t(s)$, and the expected value of carrying on. The latter pays the current cost and then discounts the next period’s value, with the expectation taken over future states given the current state $s$:

$$ \tilde V_{t+1}(s)=-c_t+\gamma\,\mathbb{E}_s\left[V_{t+1}(S_{t+1})\right] $$

so the optimal value in each state is

$$ V_t(s)=\max\left\{\,g_t(s),\ \tilde V_{t+1}(s)\,\right\} $$
Symbol Meaning
$s$ Current state and information
$g_t(s)$ Payoff from acting immediately
$c_t$ Cost of continuing to search
$\gamma$ Discount factor on future payoff
$V_t(s)$ Expected value under the optimal policy

Anyone who has met a value function in reinforcement learning will recognise this. Optimal stopping is a special Markov decision process: two actions per state, stop or continue, and stopping enters a terminal state.

Why you need not cling to 37%

Change any assumption and the optimal policy changes:

Change in the problem How the optimal policy changes
Only relative ranks are observable The classical 37% rule
Absolute scores and their distribution are known A dynamic threshold based on score and remaining chances
Earlier candidates can be recalled Keep the current best and keep searching
Searching is expensive Stop earlier
The population size is unknown Decide from arrival patterns and time costs
The global best is not required Accept options above a payoff threshold
Multiple attempts and revisions are allowed Becomes a general sequential decision problem

The second row matters a lot. Gilbert and Mosteller studied the full-information best-choice problem in 1966: if candidate quality is i.i.d. with a known continuous distribution, the asymptotic optimal success probability rises from 36.79% to about 58.02%. If every option can be evaluated accurately and kept until a final choice, success is of course 100%.

Information available Asymptotic optimal success
Relative ranks only 36.79%
Absolute quality and its distribution 58.02%
All options observable before choosing 100%

Better decisions come not only from better stopping rules but from better information, better judgement, and from altering the constraints of the decision itself.

Search theory: how many apartments should you actually see

Buying property differs from the secretary problem in four conspicuous ways: the number of listings is unknown; a viewed listing can often be revisited; you can judge absolute quality roughly; and viewing costs time and energy. The better fit is search theory, classically McCall’s 1970 job-search model.

The reservation value

Let the value of an opportunity be a random variable $X$, let the best option you can keep be worth $b$, and let one more search cost $c$. The expected incremental value of searching once more is

$$ \begin{aligned} \Delta V(b)&=\mathbb{E}\left[\max(X,b)-b\right]\\ &=\mathbb{E}\left[(X-b)^+\right] \end{aligned} $$

where $(X-b)^+=\max(X-b,0)$. If opportunity values follow a distribution $F(x)$, then

$$ \Delta V(b)=\int_b^{\infty}\left[1-F(x)\right]\mathrm{d}x $$

Under the classical conditions — i.i.d. draws, fixed search cost, the current best kept — the stopping threshold $b^*$ satisfies

$$ \mathbb{E}\left[(X-b^*)^+\right]=c $$

This $b^*$ is the reservation value; in a job search it is the reservation wage. Once the current opportunity clears it, carrying further search costs no longer pays.

A worked example

Let quality be uniform on 0 to 100, $X\sim U(0,100)$. Then

$$ \Delta V(b)=\int_b^{100}\frac{x-b}{100}\,\mathrm{d}x=\frac{(100-b)^2}{200} $$

Setting this equal to the search cost $c$:

$$ b^*=100-\sqrt{200c} $$

With a search cost equivalent to 2 points, the threshold is 80. Holding an option above 80, another search no longer covers its cost.

Same neighbourhood, quality still uniform on 0 to 100, but two different people.

One lives nearby: a ten-minute drive to each viewing, so the time and effort of one more search is worth about 2 points. Plugging into $b^*=100-\sqrt{200c}$, their reservation value is 80. A house below 80 is worth one more look; above 80, they sign.

Another flies in from out of town: every viewing takes leave, a train ticket and a hotel night, worth about 12.5 points. The same formula gives

$$ b^*=100-\sqrt{200\times 12.5}=100-50=50 $$

so their reservation value is just 50. A 65-point house is not good enough for the first buyer, but the second should already accept it.

Both look at the same homes with the same judgement. The only difference is search cost. Multiply the cost more than sixfold and the reasonable standard falls by 30 points. So “how many should I see before deciding” has no universal answer — it depends on who you are, where you are, and how much time you have. The higher the search cost, the sooner you accept good enough.

The model yields four conclusions with mathematical backing: cheaper search justifies chasing higher quality; a stronger current option shrinks the gain from continuing; a tighter deadline pushes you to accept good enough; and a more favourable distribution of future opportunities raises the acceptance standard.

Loading interactive demo…

So “look at a hundred” is not a derived result but a rule of thumb about gathering enough information. The real principle is the balance of marginal benefit and marginal cost, and that threshold depends on the quality distribution, the cost of viewing, your judgement, and what you already hold. Change the city, the budget or the timeline and the number changes too.

The value of information: why big decisions deserve research

Searching is not only about finding a better option; it can also be about improving your ability to evaluate the options you already have. These are different problems.

Viewing the fiftieth apartment, you may not like it at all, yet its transaction price, finish and location sharpen your read on the previous forty-nine. That viewing still produced value.

The definition

Let $a$ be an action, $\theta$ an uncertain state, $U(a,\theta)$ the payoff. Without new information the best expected payoff is

$$ V_0=\max_a \mathbb{E}_\theta\left[U(a,\theta)\right] $$

After observing $Y$ you can re-decide:

$$ V_1=\mathbb{E}_Y\left[\max_a \mathbb{E}_{\theta\mid Y}\left[U(a,\theta)\right]\right] $$

The expected value of the information is the difference:

$$ \mathrm{EVSI}=V_1-V_0 $$

EVSI stands for expected value of sample information. As long as the cost of acquiring it stays below this, further information is worth paying for.

Why property deserves many viewings and a jacket does not

Suppose research lets you avoid a loss equal to 5% of the transaction value:

Decision Amount involved Loss potentially avoided
A jacket ¥500 ¥25
A phone ¥6,000 ¥300
A car ¥300,000 ¥15,000
An apartment ¥5,000,000 ¥250,000
A long-term career choice Millions in income and opportunity Potentially very large

The 5% is illustrative, not a statistical finding. But it points at a principle: research effort should be matched to the long-term impact and irreversibility of the decision.

Many people do the reverse — hours of comparison shopping for a cheap item, then a single impression to choose a job, a city or a career. From an information-economics view, that is inefficient allocation of decision resources.

Explore versus exploit: why youth should widen the sample

Optimal stopping assumes that choosing ends the process. Life is not like that: you can take a job and then switch, try a model and then adjust, learn a skill and then pivot.

  • Exploration: try unknown options, gain information, discover higher payoffs.
  • Exploitation: concentrate resources on known good options and collect steady returns.

This is the central tension of reinforcement learning and the multi-armed bandit. The classic UCB rule scores each option as

$$ a_t=\arg\max_i\left[\underbrace{\hat{\mu}_i}_{\text{estimated payoff}}+\underbrace{c\sqrt{\frac{\ln t}{n_i}}}_{\text{exploration bonus}}\right] $$

where $n_i$ is how often option $i$ has been tried. A direction with a modest estimated payoff can still deserve priority if it has barely been sampled and remains uncertain. This is one mathematical basis for widening your sample of life.

Loading interactive demo…

UCB does carry specific statistical assumptions, and a career is not a stationary, independent bandit. What is worth borrowing is the joint consideration of potential payoff and uncertainty.

Exploration is not free. Skills, networks, capital and reputation compound, captured crudely by

$$ K_{t+1}=(1-\delta)K_t+I_t $$

Switching directions depreciates the old $K$ at rate $\delta$ and restarts the new one from zero. The ideal is therefore not “explore when young, exploit when old” but one direction that produces steady returns, with a standing budget for trying new ones.

Applied to concrete decisions

Housing: build a benchmark, then recognise the opportunity

First-time buyers hit two problems: they don’t know what a fair price is, and they don’t know what they actually want. A more disciplined process has three stages.

Stage one, broad sampling. Learn about districts, prices, layouts, building ages, management and commuting. Don’t transact; the task is market literacy and clarifying your real requirements.

Stage two, narrowing. Rule out listings that fail hard constraints, build a valuation standard from actual transaction prices, and stop adding volume blindly in favour of targeted search.

Stage three, decide on preset conditions. When a listing meets core needs, the price is reasonable, title and quality checks pass, and further search has limited incremental value, consider buying.

Thirty representative apartments may beat a hundred near-identical ones. This is the statistical question of sample representativeness: effective sample size matters more than raw count.

Job search: don’t lock in early, don’t chase forever

Suppose you expect to see 30 potential roles during campus recruiting. The secretary-problem lesson is not to commit to the first firm too early, but to use interviews, conversations and salary discussions to learn how the market prices you.

A weighted evaluation model helps:

Dimension Example weight
Long-term career growth 30%
Compensation and benefits 25%
Industry prospects 20%
Team and technical level 15%
Work-life balance 10%

Composite utility is

$$ U_i=\sum_{j=1}^{m}w_jx_{ij} $$

where $w_j$ is the weight of dimension $j$ and $x_{ij}$ is offer $i$’s score on it. Under these weights, an offer scoring 90, 85, 90, 80, 60 comes to 84.3. Both weights and scores are illustrative: set your own and audit hard constraints separately.

Loading interactive demo…

Real job searches differ from the secretary problem: offers expire, and several processes can run in parallel. So beyond optimising the stopping rule, change the rules — ask for extensions, run interviews concurrently, line offers up in the same window. Increasing how many opportunities you can hold at once often beats fine-tuning when to stop.

Partners: learn your preferences, don’t chase a global optimum

Partner choice is often used to illustrate the secretary problem: search from 20 to 30, so the 37% rule says end the observation phase around 23.7. That inference is loose, because intimate relationships violate the assumptions badly:

Secretary problem Partner choice in reality
Fixed number of candidates Unknown how many you will meet
Fixed candidate quality People grow and change
Unilateral choice Mutual selection
Quality judged immediately Deep traits need time together
A single ranking Values, temperament and goals are multidimensional
Payoff fixed once chosen Relationship quality is built jointly

What transfers is this: before committing long term, meet a range of people through real social life and learn your own preferences, boundaries and core needs. But there is no reason to deliberately reject the first 37%, and certainly no reason to abandon a good relationship because a theoretically better partner might exist. Partner choice is less about taking the maximum from a pool than about finding someone long-term compatible and building value together.

Investing: act after research, don’t wait for the perfect entry

The familiar bind: buy now and it may fall tomorrow; wait and it may run away.

Holding cash preserves the option to invest later, but waiting carries opportunity cost in appreciation, dividends and compounding. One important improvement is to avoid a single all-in decision. Staged entry, regular investing and target allocations convert a hard one-shot stopping problem into a staged one.

For long-term index investing, hunting the absolute bottom is not a sensible objective. For individual stocks, thresholds based on valuation, fundamentals and risk usually beat mechanically waiting for some fraction of time to elapse.

Career: when to stop exploring and go deep

Probably the most useful application for younger readers. Suppose four directions: build expertise in a mature industry, enter a fast-growing technology field, start a company, or build an audience as a creator.

Careers differ because payoffs are not fixed: time invested builds capability, network and resources, which reshape future payoff distributions. The equation $K_{t+1}=(1-\delta)K_t+I_t$ is the reminder that frequent switching raises learning costs and destroys accumulation.

A reasonable arrangement runs a core direction alongside exploration. 70/20/10 is a workable example: 70% into the core for capability and long-term returns, 20% into adjacent exploration, 10% into cross-domain bets with non-linear upside. It is not a proven optimum, but it maintains accumulation without foreclosing discovery.

Loading interactive demo…

Changing the problem beats solving it

The rules of the secretary problem cannot be changed. In life they usually can:

Original problem How to change the decision structure
Must decide on the spot Prepare valuation, financing and due diligence in advance
Offer about to expire Ask for an extension, interview in parallel
Unsure about a career switch Ship a low-cost project or part-time trial first
Unsure about a city Live there briefly before settling
Unsure a venture will work Build an MVP to test real demand
Unsure about investing now Stagger entries rather than one decision
Unsure a research direction is viable Run a small pilot experiment

Behind this is real options theory: under uncertainty, the right to wait, scale up, scale down or exit has economic value in itself.

Rather than trying to think your way to the one correct answer, break a major irreversible decision into a series of small reversible experiments. The traditional mode is a single irreversible verdict; the sequential mode is staged commitment with continuously updated beliefs. The latter caps the cost of being wrong and uses real feedback to correct judgement.

Conclusion

After all the derivation, what deserves long-term use is not the number 37% but these six points.

  1. Make no major commitment before your evaluation criteria are reliable. With too little information you do not even know what level the current opportunity occupies.
  2. Deliberately widen your effective sample. More varied people, industries, cities and ways of living both surface opportunities and improve your evaluation system.
  3. Allocate research effort in proportion to importance. The more valuable, long-term and irreversible the decision, the more time it deserves; everything else should be finished quickly.
  4. Do not chase the global optimum; chase the expected optimum net of cost. Waiting indefinitely for a possibly better option does not necessarily raise final payoff.
  5. Convert irreversible major decisions into reversible small experiments wherever possible. Much uncertainty cannot be reasoned away, only discovered through action.
  6. Keep accumulating along one direction while retaining capacity to explore. Neither freeze so early that new possibilities vanish, nor explore so long that compounding never starts.

Point 3, allocating research effort in proportion to importance, works out in practice from just two variables: what the decision is worth, and whether a mistake can be undone. Cross them and the required density follows:

Decision type Suitable strategy
Low value, reversible Decide fast, minimise cognitive cost
Low value, irreversible Satisfy basic conditions and move on
High value, reversible Small-scale trial and error, adjust dynamically
High value, irreversible Deep research, strict stopping threshold

The cell that goes wrong is not the first but the last: something expensive that cannot be undone, handled the way the first cell is handled — decided offhandedly, then paid for over a long time.

Everything above is one tension seen from two sides: accumulating information and preserving options pull against each other, and to look at a few more you must give up a few. Deciding early pays for insufficient information; deciding late pays for opportunities lost.

The purpose of a decision is not to eliminate uncertainty, but to find, while uncertainty persists, the moment worth acting on.

Map first, then move.

item.title: Syncing Google Calendar on Xiaomi HyperOS
item.description:
Tested on 24 November 2026.

I spent half a day trying to fix Google Calendar sync on a Xiaomi phone. The Google account was already signed in, and other sync items such as contacts had recent update records. The system calendar, however, kept failing.

In the end, there was no need to fight with Google Play services or install another app. Xiaomi Calendar supports CalDAV, so connecting it directly to Google Calendar solved the problem.

Where the problem was

On the phone’s Google account sync page, two similarly named items are easy to confuse: Google Calendar and Calendar.

On my phone, the first showed a successful sync that day, while the second kept returning an error. Its last successful sync was still 24 October 2025. Google events also failed to appear in the stock Xiaomi Calendar app.

Android’s system calendar relies on a calendar sync adapter and the system calendar database. A working Google sign-in does not necessarily mean that the system calendar sync chain is healthy. I did not dig further into which component was at fault; I switched to a different sync method instead.

The fix: use Xiaomi Calendar’s built-in CalDAV support

CalDAV is an open protocol for accessing and synchronising calendars. Since Xiaomi Calendar supports it and Google Calendar exposes a CalDAV interface, it is possible to bypass the original Google account calendar sync mechanism.

All you need is a Google app-specific password and the CalDAV server address.

1. Generate a Google app-specific password

First, open Google Account security settings and confirm that two-step verification is enabled.

Then open the app passwords page and create a new password. The app name can be Xiaomi Calendar.

Google will generate a 16-character app-specific password. Copy it for later use and remove the spaces when entering it.

Note that this is an app-specific password, not the password for your Google account. If you stop using this sync setup later, you can revoke that password separately in your Google account.

2. Add a CalDAV account in Xiaomi Calendar

Open the stock Calendar app on the Xiaomi phone and go through:

three-dot menu at the top right → Settings → Calendar account management → Import account → Import CalDAV account

Then fill in the following fields. Assume the Google email address is example@gmail.com:

Field Value
Username example@gmail.com
Password The 16-character app-specific password just generated
Server address https://www.google.com/calendar/dav/example@gmail.com/user/

The server address can be copied from the line below:

1

https://www.google.com/calendar/dav/example@gmail.com/user/

Replace example@gmail.com with your own Google email address, make sure the phone can reach Google services, and sign in.

After the account is added, go back to Xiaomi Calendar and check whether Google events have appeared. I succeeded with Google’s legacy CalDAV endpoint.

The main trap: old and new Google CalDAV endpoints

Much of the time I lost came from Google having changed its CalDAV interface.

Legacy endpoint:

1

https://www.google.com/calendar/dav/

Current endpoint:

1

https://apidata.googleusercontent.com/caldav/v2/

According to the official Google developer guide, the legacy endpoint has been deprecated and is no longer supported. The current endpoint requires OAuth 2.0 and does not support traditional Basic Authentication.

Xiaomi Calendar’s CalDAV import screen, however, only offers a server address, username and password. There is no Google OAuth authorisation flow. As a result, copying the current endpoint from the official documentation cannot solve the authentication problem.

When I saw that the legacy endpoint had been deprecated, I assumed this route was closed. In practice, as of 24 November 2026, the legacy endpoint still connected and successfully synced my Google events to the Xiaomi phone.

Deprecation does not necessarily mean that a service has already been shut down. Still, because Google no longer offers official support, this method may stop working in the future, and it is not guaranteed to work for every account or system version.

Is manual syncing needed afterwards?

CalDAV is different from a one-off ICS import. It supports ongoing synchronisation and can read and write events in both directions.

How Xiaomi Calendar performs background sync, how often it runs, and whether local edits are written back to Google Calendar still depend on the client implementation. What I confirmed was that the account connected and events were fetched. I have not yet verified long-term automatic syncing or two-way writes.

You can enable automatic sync of data in the phone settings, allow Xiaomi Calendar to use the network in the background, and make sure background network access to Google services works. Then create a Google event on a computer and see whether it appears on the phone automatically. That will tell you whether background syncing is working.

If the original Google Calendar sync starts working again, check for duplicate events and hide or disable the older sync source if necessary.

After half a day, the built-in feature in Xiaomi Calendar was what solved the problem. If you run into the same situation, try CalDAV before turning to more complicated solutions. At least in this test, no rooting, flashing or extra app installation was needed.

References: Google CalDAV API developer guide · Google app-specific password help

item.title: The AI Era Is Almost the Era of Lean Muscle
item.description:
For young people, the AI era is almost the era of lean muscle. AI is changing three things at once: the relative price of standardized cognitive output, the way people are tied to work, and the cost of looking after one’s body. Taken together, these changes make it worthwhile to move physical training up the list of things that used to come after work.

Ordinary, easily copied cognitive work will lose value quickly

When the reaper arrived, people who swung scythes did not become weaker. But harvesting the same amount of grain no longer required as many workers. Every technological shift makes some paid tasks cheaper and turns other abilities or resources into new bottlenecks. Here is one way to look at the transition from agriculture to the AI era.

Transition What gets cheaper What becomes scarce What not to bet on What to build
Agriculture → industry Repetitive physical work that can be mechanized Machines, capital, and the ability to organize production at scale More effort and longer hours Operate and maintain equipment; organize people to produce with it
Industry → information age Routine tasks that can be written as rules Turning business processes into software and using data to solve complex problems Memorizing procedures, manual spreadsheets, repetitive data entry Turn recurring processes into tools and handle exceptions
Information age → AI era First drafts of cognitive work that can be described in natural language and checked quickly Defining problems, verifying what ships, taking responsibility for results, proprietary data, and customer access Hand-writing every line of code, piling up deliverables, proving commitment by sitting at a desk Build judgment through practice, hand repetitive work to agents, and save time for your body

  • Machines took over hand harvesting and carrying. Software took over manual bookkeeping, order entry, and reports assembled from fixed templates. The share of the U.S. workforce employed in agriculture fell from about 41% in 1900 to 1.9% in 2000. Mechanization alone did not cause this, and these figures do not measure farm workers’ wage losses, but they show the scale of labor moving out of agriculture.

  • Computers reduced the labor needed for routine manual and cognitive tasks while increasing the relative demand for nonroutine cognitive work.

  • The most important difference with AI is this: software used to need rules written into it before it could act. Now, if a goal can be explained and the result checked, some work can go to an agent even when it is hard to describe with a complete set of rules.

Coding agents are starting to change how internet companies think about staffing. Fixing bugs, adding tests, and building small features used to mean adding people. Now an engineer who knows the business can hand several tasks to different agents to work on in parallel, then review the results. Over the next few years, junior roles focused mainly on execution may feel the pressure first. In 2026, AI has begun taking part in research on frontier mathematics, with research teams reporting solutions to open problems.

  • Some work that once needed a large team may shift to a few core engineers and several agents. Core engineers decide what to build, judge whether the results are ready to ship, and take responsibility for them. For young people, opportunities to develop that judgment may become the scarce resource.

  • The code and documents belong to the company. Your lean muscle belongs to you. Work products need to be handed over. Your physique does not.

Across five thousand years, power and sexual appeal remain reliable answers

Technology changes, as do the things we can mass-produce, but two abilities are harder to copy. One is deciding what other people get. The other is making people willing to pay a price to get close to you. The first is power. The second is attraction, with sexual appeal as one direct form of it.

Power

  • During the Warring States period, Lü Buwei bet on the offices Zichu might one day award. When Zichu was still a hostage in Zhao, Lü judged him a “rare commodity,” spent money cultivating contacts, and arranged for people to persuade Lady Huayang to make him heir. Once Zichu took the throne, Lü became chancellor.
  • Today, someone seeking promotion might first give a gift to Yu Lifang, the wife of a senior official. She held no formal human-resources post, yet could directly approach provincial and municipal leaders to seek promotions for others. Others competed for a place on the list; she could influence the list.

Sexual appeal | From being noticed to getting what others cannot

  • In ancient China, Emperor Xuanzong favored Yang Guifei. Her three sisters were made ladies of the state, and her cousin Yang Guozhong rose to prominence. What mattered was not that everyone found her beautiful, but that the person who did could bring status to her family.
  • Today, people may spend money without ever meeting in person. OnlyFans creator Sophie Rain said that one fan she knew only through the platform had spent nearly $5 million on her over 11 months. Some pay to view content; others pay for a few more replies from her.

Power decides who gets to make the call. Sexual appeal can make people come closer, even spend money. But there is a more direct reason the body is valuable: even if nobody is watching, the strength you build is still yours to use.

You can check in with an agent between sets, so training need not interrupt work

Work and training used to collide because many tasks could only move forward at a computer. When an experiment finished, I had to inspect the results, change parameters, and submit the next run myself. Now I can finish a set of rows, pick up my phone during the rest, check what an agent just completed, and reply, “Keep the original data split and add a comparison.” I put the phone away and do the next set; the agent keeps editing code and running experiments remotely. I need a few seconds to make a decision, not to sit back down at a computer and do the whole next round from scratch.

This is no longer just hypothetical. With Codex, for example, you can send instructions from your phone, adjust a running task, and review changes and test results. Sending an instruction, answering a clear question, or checking an interim result can fit into a rest period. Close code review, diagnosing an anomaly, and taking responsibility for final acceptance can wait until I am back at my computer. Not every task belongs on a phone, but many no longer need to wait for me to return to my desk before they can move forward.

That gives me one less excuse to put off going to the gym. I used to think I had to finish this round before leaving. Now I can go train, then check in when an agent finishes if I have time between sets. I keep training, and work keeps moving. What shrinks is the time I have to spend at my computer.

AI narrows information gaps, helping ordinary people train and eat well

You may not need a coach or nutritionist to train and eat better now. If I can get to the gym only two evenings a week, I can send my training log to AI and ask what to do next time. At lunch, I can send it the cafeteria menu and ask how to put this meal together, instead of receiving a meal plan I cannot use.

The internet has never lacked workout tutorials. What is missing is someone who can tell me what to do today with my schedule, the equipment I have, and the dishes in front of me. AI narrows that information gap. If an ordinary person wants to start, they can do a set and put together a good meal today. The hardest part is still doing it again tomorrow.

Why muscle, and why lean?

Muscle is function. The benefits of resistance training are practical: building muscle can support metabolism, protect body tissues, and make the body more resilient.

For young people just starting their careers, these years may be their last golden window for building muscle. After graduation, commuting, overtime, meals, and sleep are all being rearranged. If training is always scheduled for “after work is done today,” a few years can turn into a habit of waiting until life gets less busy. If instead you treat two or three weekly sessions as part of a normal schedule, what you build over these years is not just muscle and strength, but also a routine you know how to keep when work gets busy.

Lean means low maintenance, leaving the main plot of life intact. Defined shoulders, back, and waist, plus a strong body, can be maintained with a few workouts a week and ordinary meals. When work gets busy, you can train less for a while; when traveling, you do not have to plan every day around a gym.

Managing blood sugar and body fat has direct benefits, too: it may help reduce inflammation and metabolic risk, lower the risk of cavities, and make muscle definition more visible.

item.title: Understanding a Job Offer in China: Pay, Benefits and Take-home Income
item.description:
One offer advertises RMB 700,000 in annual compensation; another offers RMB 430,000 plus extra insurance and a pension plan. The headline figures are easy to compare, but the money works differently: some arrives monthly, some depends on performance, some is held in benefit accounts, and some is an equity valuation that may never become cash.

This guide builds a practical ledger for offers in Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen, Hangzhou and Quanzhou, including technology companies, state-owned enterprises and research institutions. All offers and calculations are hypothetical; policy references were checked on 9 November 2026. Local rules and individual circumstances matter.

Five layers of an offer

Layer Examples What to check
Fixed cash Monthly salary and explicitly guaranteed pay Contract, payment dates, probation terms
Variable cash Annual, quarterly and project bonuses Targets, performance rules and past payouts
Benefits Employer housing-fund contributions, annuity and medical cover Employer cost, vesting and access
One-off payments Signing, relocation and retention bonuses Payment dates, tax and clawback
Equity Shares, restricted stock units and options Vesting, price, exercise and liquidity

These have different certainty, liquidity and risk. Employer social-insurance contributions provide protection and are part of employment cost; they are not simply wages in hand. Employee contributions already come from gross salary and should not be counted again as an extra employer benefit.

1. Fixed cash: base pay and after-tax salary

Monthly salary, fixed pay and total compensation

Base usually means fixed gross pay, although the contract’s “basic salary” can be only one component. Check whether allowances, position pay and monthly performance pay are guaranteed.

Total compensation (TC) commonly includes base, target bonus and equity, but the employer defines its quoted scope. RMB 420,000 fixed pay + RMB 140,000 target bonus + RMB 120,000 of equity scheduled to vest gives a target TC of RMB 680,000; only RMB 420,000 is fixed cash. Keep target, realized compensation and total employer cost distinct.

A raise changes future base pay: a 10% increase from RMB 40,000 to RMB 44,000 per month adds RMB 48,000 to annual fixed pay while it remains in force. A RMB 48,000 bonus is a one-time payment.

Income tax: marginal is not average

Chinese resident individuals’ comprehensive income is taxed progressively. Annual taxable income generally deducts the RMB 60,000 basic allowance, eligible social-insurance and housing-fund contributions, special additional deductions and other allowable items.

Annual taxable income (RMB) Rate Quick deduction (RMB)
Up to 36,000 3% 0
36,000–144,000 10% 2,520
144,000–300,000 20% 16,920
300,000–420,000 25% 31,920
420,000–660,000 30% 52,920
660,000–960,000 35% 85,920
Above 960,000 45% 181,920

Salary tax and special additional deductions

Annual taxable comprehensive income generally equals annual comprehensive income less the RMB 60,000 basic allowance, eligible social-insurance and housing-fund contributions, special additional deductions and other lawful deductions. Tax then follows the applicable rate and quick deduction. The RMB 60,000 is an allowance in the calculation, not cash paid to the employee. Comprehensive income may include labor remuneration, authors’ remuneration and royalties, with income amounts determined under the applicable rules.

The seven common special additional deductions, subject to eligibility, are care of children under three, children’s education, continuing education, major medical expenses, housing-loan interest, housing rent and support for elderly dependants. Each has its own eligibility, limits and filing requirements.

For eligible rent, Beijing, Shanghai, Guangzhou, Shenzhen and Hangzhou generally use RMB 1,500 per month; other cities follow the applicable city category. An RMB 18,000 annual deduction entirely within a 25% marginal bracket reduces tax by RMB 4,500, not RMB 18,000. If the deduction crosses brackets, calculate savings in stages. Restrictions also apply to an individual and spouse claiming rent and mortgage interest; see the tax authority’s rent guidance.

The seven deductions: amounts and eligibility

The table reflects publicly available rules checked on 9 November 2026. Amounts reduce taxable income when the conditions are met; they are not cash reimbursements or direct tax refunds.

Deduction Main amount Eligibility and allocation
Care of a child under three RMB 2,000 per child per month From birth month through the month before age three; one parent may claim 100% or each 50%, with the method fixed for the tax year
Children’s education RMB 2,000 per child per month Qualifying preschool and full-time education; one parent may claim 100% or each 50%, with the method fixed for the tax year
Continuing education Eligible domestic degree education: RMB 400/month, up to 48 months per degree; eligible professional qualification: RMB 3,600 in the year the certificate is obtained Rules depend on the type, certificate and duration. For eligible undergraduate-or-lower continuing education, the individual or a parent may claim under the rules, without double counting
Major medical expenses Eligible out-of-pocket expenses after basic medical reimbursement above RMB 15,000, up to RMB 80,000 per patient per year Limited to qualifying in-catalog expenses; the taxpayer or spouse can claim an adult’s expense, one parent can claim a minor child’s expense, and each patient’s amount is calculated separately at annual settlement
Housing-loan interest RMB 1,000/month for eligible first-home loan interest, at most 240 months Qualifying interest must actually arise; spouses normally choose one claimant, with special rules for qualifying loans each obtained before marriage
Housing rent RMB 1,500, 1,100 or 800/month according to the main work city’s category The taxpayer must have no owned home in the main work city and meet other conditions; spouses in the same main work city can claim only once, and rent and mortgage deductions have allocation restrictions
Support for elderly dependants Only child: RMB 3,000/month; others share RMB 3,000/month with siblings, capped at RMB 1,500 per person An eligible dependant includes a parent aged 60 or over; agreed or designated sharing requires written documentation and the method and amount are fixed for the tax year

Sources: childcare and education, continuing education and medical expenses, medical deduction claimants, mortgage interest, rent and elder care. A parent’s pension income does not by itself disqualify a qualifying elder-care deduction; a parent’s medical expenses cannot simply be claimed as the child’s major-medical deduction.

For example, if one patient’s eligible in-catalog annual out-of-pocket amount after reimbursement is RMB 30,000, the amount above RMB 15,000 is RMB 15,000. If it is RMB 110,000, the excess is RMB 95,000 but the deductible amount is capped at RMB 80,000 for that patient. Eligibility depends on records and tax rules.

Calculate savings on the same salary: deductions can cross brackets

Assume a Beijing employee earns RMB 480,000 annual fixed wages, RMB 98,175.60 employee insurance and housing-fund contributions, and a RMB 60,000 basic allowance. The RMB 120,000 bonus is assumed to qualify for separate bonus taxation. Looking at salary alone, with no other income or deductions:

Scenario Special additional deduction Taxable salary Salary tax Saving versus no deduction
None RMB 0 RMB 321,824.40 RMB 48,536.10 —
Qualifying rent RMB 18,000/year RMB 303,824.40 RMB 44,036.10 RMB 4,500.00
Rent plus one child’s education, both lawfully claimed in full by this taxpayer RMB 42,000/year RMB 279,824.40 RMB 39,044.88 RMB 9,491.22

The final saving is not 42,000 × 25% = RMB 10,500: the deduction crosses the RMB 300,000 threshold. RMB 21,824.40 saves tax at 25% and the remaining RMB 20,175.60 at 20%. This describes the calculation across brackets, not separate policy rates for rent and education. Eligibility and family allocation must be checked individually.

Why does monthly withholding change when salary stays the same?

Salary generally uses cumulative withholding: the current month’s withholding equals cumulative tax due through that month less previous withholding. Assume RMB 40,000 salary, RMB 8,181.30 employee social-insurance and housing-fund contributions and RMB 5,000 basic allowance every month, with no special additional deductions or other changes. Cumulative taxable income grows by RMB 26,818.70 each month.

Month Cumulative taxable income Cumulative withholding due Current month’s withholding
1 RMB 26,818.70 RMB 804.56 RMB 804.56
2 RMB 53,637.40 RMB 2,843.74 RMB 2,039.18
6 RMB 160,912.20 RMB 15,262.44 RMB 4,373.09
12 RMB 321,824.40 RMB 48,536.10 RMB 6,454.96

Each current-month amount subtracts the immediately preceding month’s cumulative withholding, even if that month is not shown. Changes in salary, contributions or deductions change actual withholding. Annual settlement considers all comprehensive income and prior withholding. A qualifying bonus separately taxed under the rules is excluded from the salary table.

Filing and annual settlement
  • Enter the deduction year and required details in the individual income-tax app or natural-person e-tax system. Eligible deductions can generally be claimed through payroll withholding or in annual settlement; major medical expenses are claimed in annual settlement.
  • Coordinate allocations with a spouse or siblings, update changes in leases, education and family circumstances, and keep required contracts, receipts or sharing agreements.
  • When comprehensive-income settlement is required, the normal filing window is 1 March through 30 June of the following year. Not everyone must file; the settlement rules describe required and exempt cases.
  • Eligible deductions omitted earlier may be added under the rules at settlement. A refund is calculated from annual tax due versus tax already withheld; it is not the deduction amount itself. Applicable underpayment must also be handled according to the rules. See deductions that may be added.

Other lawful deductions are distinct from the seven special additional deductions. For example, contributions to a personal pension funding account can be deducted as paid up to RMB 12,000 per year, subject to the rules. Access is restricted and investment returns and withdrawals have separate tax treatment; the deduction amount is not itself the tax saving. Tax authority guidance.

Reaching the 30% bracket does not tax all income at 30%. Monthly payroll generally uses cumulative withholding; withholding may rise later in the year, followed by an annual settlement where applicable.

2. Variable cash: performance and bonuses

How much of an extra salary multiple is paid?

“35k × 16” implies RMB 560,000: RMB 420,000 over 12 months plus a target four-month bonus of RMB 140,000. Suppose that bonus is multiplied by performance factor \(K\):

Factor Gross annual cash Equivalent months
0 RMB 420,000 12
0.5 RMB 490,000 14
1 RMB 560,000 16
1.5 RMB 630,000 18

Adjust the hypothetical performance factor to see gross annual cash and equivalent salary months. Actual bonus rules depend on the employer.

Loading interactive example…

Actual rules vary. Ask how many months are guaranteed, what the target is and what was historically paid. Performance grades have no universal meaning and may affect bonuses, raises, promotion and equity refreshes. A performance improvement plan (PIP) does not automatically mean immediate dismissal.

How is the annual bonus taxed?

The annual one-off bonus policy runs through 31 December 2027: qualifying bonuses may be taxed separately or included in comprehensive income. The separate method is available once per tax year. The better choice depends on individual circumstances. A signing or quarterly bonus does not automatically qualify merely because it is paid once.

For separate taxation, divide the qualifying bonus by 12 to find the monthly rate and quick deduction, then calculate total bonus × rate − quick deduction. For a RMB 120,000 bonus, 120,000 / 12 = RMB 10,000, corresponding to 10% and RMB 210, so tax is RMB 11,790 and the net bonus is RMB 108,210.

At some thresholds, a slightly larger bonus can result in lower net pay because the rate applied to the whole bonus changes. Compare separate and combined taxation against full-year income and deductions; do not assume all one-off payments qualify.

Payment timing matters too. The same annual amount paid monthly provides a different cash flow from a large performance-dependent year-end payment. Avoid budgeting regular expenses against a bonus that has not yet been earned.

3. Benefits and protection: social insurance and long-term benefits

Social insurance and the housing fund

The five social-insurance categories are pension, medical, unemployment, work injury and maternity insurance. The housing provident fund is separate. Employees and employers generally contribute to pension, medical and unemployment insurance; employers normally fund work-injury and maternity insurance. Rates, medical tiers and contribution bases vary by location.

What the five insurances cover

Scheme Employee Employer Purpose
Pension Commonly 8% of assessed base Local statutory rate Personal and pooled components support retirement benefits
Medical Generally contributes; local tiers vary Local rate Personal-account and pooled benefits have different rules and reimbursement limits
Unemployment Generally contributes; rates vary Local rate Protection when eligibility conditions are met
Work injury Normally no contribution Contributes at the applicable rate Eligible work-related injury and medical benefits; rates can vary by industry
Maternity Normally no contribution Contributes under local rules Eligible maternity medical expenses and allowances; often administered with medical insurance

These are common employee arrangements; consult the local rules. Statutory coverage applies during probation too. Lower contributions can increase current cash without necessarily improving protection.

Pension: income after retirement

At an assessed RMB 20,000 base, the employee’s 8% contribution is RMB 1,600 and the employer’s 16% is RMB 3,200. The employee contribution enters the personal account; the employer contribution generally enters a pooled fund. Benefits depend on contribution history, assessed wages, location and personal account. The personal-account component generally divides the account balance by the applicable calculation months; the basic component is calculated separately.

Under the gradual retirement reform, the minimum contribution period for monthly basic pension rises by six months each year from 2030, reaching 20 years in 2039. Other requirements, including retirement age, also apply.

Medical: outpatient, hospital and medicines

Personal-account funds can be used for eligible care and prescriptions and, subject to rules, family sharing. The pooled fund pays eligible costs. As an illustration, if RMB 8,000 of a RMB 10,000 bill is covered, a hypothetical RMB 1,000 deductible and 80% reimbursement produce RMB 5,600 from the pooled fund; the remaining RMB 4,400 is borne by the individual or other channels. These are explanatory assumptions, not a city’s benefit schedule.

Unemployment: a buffer when income stops

Eligible workers can receive unemployment insurance benefits and related medical coverage. Conditions generally include at least one year of contributions, involuntary termination, registration and a willingness to seek work; the agency determines eligibility. Resigning voluntarily usually does not satisfy the involuntary-termination condition, though specific circumstances matter.

The benefit is not a fixed percentage of former pay. For benefits from September 2026, Shenzhen pays RMB 2,430 per month, 90% of its RMB 2,700 minimum wage; duration depends on applicable rules.

Work injury and maternity: employer-funded benefits

Work-injury insurance can cover eligible medical treatment, rehabilitation, disability and death benefits. Wages and benefits during an approved work-injury leave period are handled under applicable rules. Maternity insurance covers eligible medical expenses and maternity allowances. Male employees are also covered under the scheme; personal and spouse benefits depend on local rules. These contributions are normally paid by employers, not employees.

The general formula is monthly contribution = assessed base × contribution rate. The base often reflects prior-year wage income and is subject to local floors and ceilings; rules for new employees may differ. Social insurance and housing funds can have different bases, caps and adjustment dates.

Employee pension contributions create personal-account entitlements; employer contributions generally go to a pooled fund. Medical insurance also has personal and pooled components. These are protections and future entitlements, not an ordinary cash deposit.

Both employee and employer housing-fund contributions enter the employee’s account, subject to withdrawal and loan rules. At a hypothetical RMB 30,000 monthly base and equal rates:

Employee + employer rate Employee / month Employer / month Annual account increase
5% + 5% RMB 1,500 RMB 1,500 RMB 36,000
7% + 7% RMB 2,100 RMB 2,100 RMB 50,400

How to check whether an employer contributes correctly

  1. Keep the contract, payslips and bonus records; determine prior-year assessable wages under local rules. New employees can have different assessment rules.
  2. Check location, coverage, months, assessed bases and payment records through the national social-insurance service or local agencies. Check housing-fund bases, rates and employer deposits through the local fund center.
  3. Compare the legally assessed wage against each scheme’s local floor and ceiling. A minimum base is not automatically unlawful; it depends on the assessed wage and applicable rules.
  4. Ask HR for the calculation if records differ. If unresolved, contact the social-insurance, medical-insurance or housing-fund agency, or 12333. Keep the supporting records.

The obligation to pay statutory social insurance cannot simply be waived by agreement; see the Supreme People’s Court interpretation.

How to withdraw housing funds in six cities

Contribution amounts are not automatically spendable cash. The comparison below uses common employee cases and policies available through 9 November 2026. In Shenzhen, the “monthly contribution due” includes both employer and employee. If each contributes RMB 4,800, the total is RMB 9,600; 80% gives an illustrative RMB 7,680/month for eligible months in the temporary policy period. Actual availability depends on the eligible months, account balance and assessment. Shenzhen’s explanation.

Home purchase, repayment and other withdrawals
  • Beijing: A qualifying purchase using a Beijing center housing-fund loan, including a combined loan, can be handled under the purchase-withdrawal guide. Eligible local owner-occupied renovation may also be claimed against qualifying invoices subject to limits; see the 2026 policy.
  • Shanghai: Eligible buyers of completed new commercial homes can apply to use their own and their spouse’s housing funds for a down payment, subject to registration and other restrictions in the 2026 notice. Qualifying housing-fund loans in other Yangtze River Delta provinces have a separate repayment arrangement.
  • Guangzhou: Purchase and loan-repayment withdrawal conditions differ by property location, purchase and loan status. Eligible local buyers can apply for a down-payment withdrawal; see the center’s service materials and city service overview. The proposal to allow purchases throughout China remains a consultation draft in the material checked.
  • Shenzhen: For eligible down-payment withdrawals, a first-home claim cannot exceed account balance or down payment; a second-home claim cannot exceed 60% of account balance or the down payment. See the housing authority’s explanation. Eligible employees can sign a repayment withdrawal agreement for monthly payments.
  • Hangzhou: Eligible purchase and repayment withdrawals follow applicable rules. For a local owner-occupied purchase, the employee and spouse may claim qualifying deed tax up to the actual tax paid, under the 2026 notice.
  • Quanzhou: For qualifying purchases of owner-occupied housing in Fujian, the buyer’s and spouse’s parents and children may apply for intergenerational support withdrawal under the rules. Resale housing, mortgages and supervised accounts have distinct conditions; see the center’s explanation.

Leaving a job, retirement, settling abroad and other locally defined cases may involve account suspension, transfer or closing withdrawal. Leaving a job does not automatically permit immediate withdrawal of the entire balance. Check the specific fund center, including any provincial or central branch, account status, housing location and family eligibility; use the center’s official services or 12329 for documents and limits. Withdrawal can affect a housing-fund loan calculated from account balance, as in Shenzhen’s loan rules.

Housing-fund withdrawal and the tax rent deduction in section 1 are different systems. A withdrawal moves eligible money from the worker’s fund account; a tax deduction reduces taxable income. A RMB 2,000 housing-fund withdrawal is not a RMB 2,000 tax credit.

Supplementary insurance and annuities

“Six insurances and two funds” is not a single standardized statutory package. The extra insurance may be supplementary medical cover; the second fund may be an enterprise or occupational annuity. Check deductibles, reimbursement rates, hospital networks, family coverage and annual limits.

An enterprise annuity supplements basic pension insurance. Under the enterprise annuity rules, annual employer contributions cannot exceed 8% of the enterprise’s employee wage bill, and combined employer and employee contributions cannot exceed 12%. This does not guarantee an 8% + 4% rate for each person. At a hypothetical RMB 20,000 monthly base, 8% employer and 4% employee contributions total RMB 19,200 and RMB 9,600 a year respectively. Employer contributions may vest over time; ask what happens on departure. Occupational annuities mainly cover relevant public-sector staff; working for a state-owned enterprise does not automatically confer public-institution status or an occupational annuity.

Occupational and enterprise annuities have different institutional rules. The occupational annuity measures provide for eligible public-sector employers to contribute 8% of the wage bill and individuals 4% of their contributory wages, credited to their occupational annuity accounts under applicable rules. Employer bookkeeping and funding arrangements depend on the type of institution and applicable rules.

Annuity vesting and medical coverage

In the example above, RMB 28,800 enters the annuity account annually: RMB 19,200 from the employer and RMB 9,600 from the employee. This is a long-term pension arrangement rather than an on-demand deposit. Investment returns and vesting affect the eventual benefit. Central-enterprise guidance allows gradual vesting of employer contributions, with full vesting no later than eight years; check the employer’s plan.

Request the supplementary medical plan summary: outpatient coverage, deductible, reimbursement after basic insurance, hospitals and private departments, prescription drugs, family coverage, annual cap, waiting period and who pays the premium. A plan cannot be assigned a reliable cash value from its name alone.

4. One-off payments: signing and allowances

A signing bonus may be paid on joining, after probation or over several years, and may already be included in first-year TC. Check service requirements, payment dates, gross-versus-net clawback and the tax treatment if repayment is required. Ask separately about settling-in, relocation, rent, retention, make-whole, referral, project and research awards. Reimbursements and cash allowances do not necessarily receive the same tax treatment.

Suppose recurring target compensation is RMB 600,000 a year and signing bonuses are RMB 100,000 in year one and RMB 50,000 in year two:

The three-year target totals RMB 1.95 million, averaging RMB 650,000 a year, while the recurring target remains RMB 600,000. Compare first-year, three-year average and post-bonus pay. The illustration excludes raises, share-price changes and performance variation.

Other payments: ask about each one

Payment Purpose Questions
Settling-in or relocation Moving or joining a location Cash or reimbursement, payment schedule and repayment
Rent allowance Housing costs Duration, overlap with talent subsidies and tax
Retention bonus Staying until a specified date Eligibility, assessment and early departure
Make-whole bonus Replacing forfeited pay or equity Basis, date and service requirements
Referral, project or research award Meeting a specified target Eligibility, caps and repeatability

For a RMB 700,000 first-year offer that includes a RMB 100,000 signing bonus and RMB 600,000 recurring target pay, the bonus must not be added twice. Ask how a gross clawback interacts with tax already withheld. Cash allowances and expense reimbursements may have different tax treatment.

5. Equity: shares, RSUs and options

Shares represent ownership. Restricted stock units (RSUs) promise shares when conditions are met. Options give the right to buy shares at a set exercise price. An employee stock ownership plan (ESOP) is an arrangement whose rights depend on its documents.

Suppose an RSU grant valued at RMB 800,000 on grant is vested over four years. Equal vesting gives RMB 200,000 per year at grant-date value; a 10% / 20% / 30% / 40% schedule gives RMB 80,000 / 160,000 / 240,000 / 320,000. Actual value depends on the share price and conditions. Check treatment of unvested awards on departure and whether annual refresh grants exist.

Options require exercise costs. For 10,000 vested options with a RMB 5 strike and a realizable sale price of RMB 20, hypothetical profit before tax and fees is 10,000 × (20 − 5) = RMB 150,000; exercise requires RMB 50,000. At a private company, ask about financing, dilution, expiry, post-departure exercise windows, buybacks and exit routes. A valuation is not spendable cash without liquidity. Equity tax depends on the instrument, company and transaction timing.

How option value changes with share price

The interactive example assumes 10,000 fully vested options, a RMB 5 strike and an immediate sale at the selected price. Exercise is assumed only above the strike. The result is theoretical and excludes taxes, transaction restrictions and time value; it does not establish an actual exit opportunity.

For options, ask about the percentage of fully diluted shares, future dilution, post-departure exercise window, cash needed and the possibility of no exit. Keep illiquid private-company equity separate in a cash budget.

Under the listed-company equity incentive tax policy, qualifying income can be taxed separately using the comprehensive-income rate table through 31 December 2027; multiple qualifying awards in one tax year are combined. Certain domestically listed company awards, following required filing, may be paid over at most 36 months; departure during that period triggers payment before leaving. This installment rule cannot automatically be applied to overseas listings.

Putting the five layers together

Before signing

  2. How many salary months are guaranteed and how many depend on performance?
  3. What are the target bonus, payout rules and payment date?
  4. Is the signing bonus included in TC, paid in installments or subject to clawback?
  5. Are rent, meals, transport or talent allowances available, and on what terms?

Social insurance and housing fund

  1. Where is social insurance paid and what is each scheme’s assessed base?
  2. What are the employee and employer housing-fund rates and assessed base?
  3. Is a supplementary housing fund offered where applicable?

Other terms

  2. What are the probation duration, salary and assessment terms?
  3. What are the non-compete, penalty, service and compensation terms?
  4. What are the leave, overtime, time off, remote-work and actual hours arrangements?
